reshared_post.author_headline: CEO at McHelp I First Aid Training and Mental Health First Aid Training for companies.
reshared_post.reshared_text:
Junior developers are not allowed to use AI for coding in our teams.

That's what a CTO told me last week.

At first, that sounded backwards to me.

━━━━━

But his reasoning was simple:

If juniors don’t learn to think through problems themselves,
they never become seniors.

And right now, that pipeline is breaking.

━━━━━

Between 2023 and 2025, entry-level hiring dropped massively.
Because many companies thought AI could handle junior-level work.

Boilerplate. Simple features. Basic tasks.

But that’s exactly how developers used to learn for later.

━━━━━

Before AI:
-> Juniors wrote simple code.
-> Made mistakes.
-> Learned why things break.
-> Got better

Today:
-> AI writes the simple parts.
-> Juniors are expected to understand complex systems immediately.
-> Without the foundation.

━━━━━

The result?
• faster output today
• fewer experienced engineers tomorrow
• growing dependency on a shrinking group of seniors

You can’t skip the learning phase.

Software engineering is not typing code.
It’s understanding systems.

━━━━━

AI doesn’t remove the need for developers.
It increases the need for people who actually understand what’s happening underneath.

Strong organizations understand this.
They don’t optimize for short-term speed.
They invest in capability.

Because if you don’t grow juniors today, you won’t have seniors in five years.

author.name: Jarmo Venalainen
author.headline: Studying what AI is, what it can do and what it will do.

comments.text:
Indeed.

AI is not a shortcut that replaces learning. It’s a tool that changes where learning happens.

In real systems, juniors don’t learn by typing boilerplate. They learn by working on well-defined components inside a coherent design. Creating that clarity is the senior responsibility.

If seniors can’t define work clearly enough for juniors (with or without AI), that’s not an AI problem. That’s a leadership failure.

The useful way to think about AI coding is like a 3D printer.

The value isn’t “writing code faster.”
The value is being able to try an idea, see it run, adjust it, and try again.

That feedback loop accelerates understanding, not bypasses it.

replies.text: Yes. I'd recommend it. I've done it. I understand higher-level coding languages better because of it. A normal person buys a car to get to and from work. An engineer understands how the engine, electrical, and mechanical systems work. That's what sets us apart. If you don't want to understand how something works under the hood, that's fine, but you're not an engineer. Not every job needs an engineer, either, so that may be fine.
